61880639.title: Climate change in India
61880639.extract:
Anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions have contributed to changes in India's climate, including rising land temperatures, warming of the Indian Ocean, changes in precipitation and monsoon patterns, retreat of glaciers and changes in the Himalayan cryosphere, rising sea levels and increase in the frequency and intensity of certain extreme weather events like heatwaves, droughts, cyclones and heavy rainfall. These changes vary considerably across the country, with different regions experiencing distinct changes in climate.
India's average surface air temperature rose by around 0.89 °C during 2015–2024 relative to 1901–1930. The tropical Indian Ocean has warmed at 0.12 °C per decade since 1950. Mean southwest monsoon rainfall declined by 0.5–1.5 mm/day per decade in parts of the Indo-Gangetic Plain and northeast India during 1951–2024. North Indian Ocean sea level rose approximately 3.3 mm per year during 1993–2017.

These changes have implications for India's agriculture, water resources, ecosystems, public health and economy. India is also one of the world's largest annual greenhouse gas emitters, although its per-capita emissions remain below the global average. Coal-based electricity production, industry, transport and agriculture are among the principal sources of emissions. The country has undertaken measures to expand renewable energy, reduce the emissions intensity of its economy and adapt to climate-related risks. India has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2070.
